newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN told of violence between diplomats, NY police.
newsitem.headline: UN told of violence between diplomats, NY police.

text.p: The ambassadors of Russia and Belarus and senior New York City officials on Thursday gave conflicting accounts to a U.N. body of a recent clash between two diplomats and police.
The committee on relations with the host country reached no conclusion pending a final report promised by U.S. authorities.

Ambassadors Sergei Lavrov of Russia and Alyaksandr Sychou of Belarus said the diplomats were dragged from their parked car on Dec. 29 by two policemen who ignored their diplomatic credentials, swore at them, broke the arm of one and took them to a nearby police station in handcuffs.

But the police account, relayed to the committee, said First Secretary Boris Obnossov of Russia and Yuri Orange of Belarus attacked the policemen, who said they were parked near a fire hydrant and tried to drive away while intoxicated.

The police version was contained in a letter to the Belarus U.N. ambassador from Mayor Rudolph Giuliani, read to the committee by the New York City commissioner for the United Nations and the consular corps, Livia Sylva.

"The two New York city police officers ... deserve praise for their conduct in averting any potential tragedy ... Both Mr. Orange and Mr. Obnossov should have thanked the officers instead of attacking them," Giuliani wrote. He said the police account was borne out by seven witnesses.

Lavrov said neither diplomat was ever tested for alcohol and Orange was allowed to drive away only 30 minutes later since Obnossov's injury prevented him from taking the wheel. The ambassadors called the police action a flagrant breach of international law on the inviolability of diplomats and demanded an investigation, official apologies and disciplinary action against the policemen.

Lavrov, who also called for compensation for Obnossov's injury, broken glasses and torn clothing, said the methods used aginst him could "even be viewed in the context" of a 1984 U.N. convention against torture and other cruel or degrading treatment.
The meeting of the 15-nation committee, chaired by Ambassador Nicos Agathocleous of Cyprus, drew an unusually large crowd of diplomats and reporters.

The director of Giuliani's office of operations, Donna Lynne, said parking near a fire hydrant was a serious public safety matter. In the first six months of 1996, she said, 150 cars belonging to the Russian and Belarus U.N. missions received over 15,000 traffic tickets, none of which was paid.

In a separate incident, the State Department on Wednesday said it would ask the Georgian government to waive the immunity of a diplomat involved in a fatal five-vehicle crash in which a 16-year-old American girl was killed.
If immunity was not waived, the State Department said it expected to expel the diplomat, Gueorgui Makharadze, from the United States.
